content.text: {"relation":"REFINED","consensus_summary":"Mainstream consensus identifies heaven primarily as the transcendent dwelling place of God — his throne, presence, and glory — and derivatively as the eternal destiny/home of the redeemed. Common alternatives include the physical sky, 'kingdom of heaven' as God's reign, an intermediate state, and the newer-creation emphasis in which heaven ultimately unites with a renewed earth.","book_summary":"The book defines heaven as the jurisdiction where God's will is already done — encompassing both the visible sky and the seat of divine rule — and stresses that Scripture's saving movement runs downward, from heaven to earth, rather than upward from earth to heaven.","consensus_core_identification":"Heaven = God's dwelling/throne (the sphere of divine presence and rule) and, derivatively, the eternal home to which the redeemed go.","book_core_identification":"Heaven = the jurisdiction of God's accomplished will (seat of rule, inclusive of the visible sky), from which salvation descends to earth; it is a source of downward movement rather than an upward destination.","core_relation":"COMPATIBLE_OVERLAP","extension_relation":"PARTIAL_RECLASSIFICATION","boundary_disagreement":"The book retains the consensus's central referent (God's throne/realm of rule) but reframes the direction of eschatological hope: instead of heaven as the destination believers ascend to, heaven is the origin from which God's rule and the New Jerusalem descend. Cases the consensus treats as 'going to heaven' (eternal destiny language in John 14:2-3, Phil 3:20, 2 Cor 5:1) are reclassified under a heaven-comes-down framework. The book also deliberately fuses the 'visible sky' sense with the 'seat of rule' sense into one jurisdictional referent, where the consensus treats these as distinct senses.","material_contradiction":"None at the core. Both agree heaven is God's throne and the sphere where his will is done. The book's downward-movement emphasis contradicts only the popular derivative framing of heaven as the believers' final upward destination, and that framing is itself qualified within the consensus (the renewed-earth alternative listed as common in Responses A and C).","rationale":"The book's core — heaven as God's seat of rule where his will is already done — is squarely within the consensus's primary identification (Isa 66:1 throne language, Matt 6:10). What is materially changed is the extension and orientation: the book strips out or reframes the 'eternal destiny of the redeemed' component that the consensus makes co-primary, replacing ascent-to-heaven with descent-from-heaven (John 3:13, Rev 21:2-3). This is a genuine boundary revision — reclassifying heaven-as-destination cases — but not a replacement of the referent, since the downward/renewed-creation reading is explicitly listed as a common alternative in the blind consensus (Responses A and C). Hence REFINED rather than DIVERGENT or NOVEL.","citation_support":"STRONG","strongest_objection":"One could argue MATCH, since the book's definition (throne/rule) sits inside the consensus primary and its downward-movement emphasis matches an alternative the consensus already lists as common; on that reading the book merely selects an emphasis rather than changing extension. Alternatively, one could push toward DIVERGENT by claiming the book implicitly denies heaven as the believers' destination, a central plank of popular consensus. The middle verdict holds because the destination component is materially reweighted, but the central referent is untouched.","confidence":"high"}
